question: The trouble which broke out at yesterday’s Europa Conference League match between Club Brugge and PAOK has caused deep concern and frustration. The Belgian police used gratuitous violence against PAOK fans, firing tear gas and water cannons at them, refusing many fans entry to the stadium for no reason and arresting some of them even though they had valid tickets issued by UEFA.

It is not the first time this has happened and such behaviour undermines not only the sport itself but also the values that sport in general instils as well as the ideals of the EU, which inspire solidarity, unity and harmony among its people. Fans of all European teams are entitled to equal treatment across Europe and not be treated as second-rate fans. In view of this: 1.
How does the Commission view the unacceptable events that took place during the Club BruggePAOK game?
What can it do to ensure a coherent framework for sports fan travel that respects the rights of fans and weeds out all forms of discrimination in Europe?
answer: The Commission condemns any form of violence, in sport or elsewhere.

Whilst having no legal competence to intervene in national decisions and actions as regards public order and security, in accordance with Article 165 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU), in sport, the Commission promotes amongst others fairness and openness in sporting competitions and cooperation between bodies responsible for sports, and protects the physical and moral integrity of people in sport.

The Commission notably supports cooperation with the Council of Europe and Member States in the field of security during major sport events, football in particular, in the framework of the Saint-Denis Convention (1).

The shared project, ‘Balance S4 — Strengthening the Safety and Service pillars of the Saint-Denis Convention ’, focuses on safety and service during major sport events, promoting safer sports infrastructures, inclusion, diversity, accessibility and nondiscrimination for spectators. The duration is two years and benefits from EUR 400 000 from the Erasmus+ programme.
The project aims to exchange good practices, build a better understanding of security issues, improve spectator's experience and minimise risks during main sport events.
